demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
I remind myself it could have been worse
I dwell on what I have done wrong

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel isolated and set apart from others
The person I have become is unrecognisable to me

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only markedly high-risk/impulsive strategy and is poorly supported by the rest of the selected nodes. The other strategies are comparatively cognitive/obsessional (mental rituals, downward comparison), and the threat/memory/appraisal items do not show the broader dysregulation, dissociation, or severe affective overload that would make this combination clinically cohesive.

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Pain recall implies the patient was physically injured in the traumatic event. That is hard to reconcile with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another' unless she was also injured, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. The rest of the memory items emphasize fragmented retrieval and sensory reliving, but not a personally injured trauma narrative.

vignette:
Adaeze is a 47-year-old Nigerian-American architect, married, and until recently regarded by colleagues as one of the most meticulous and composed professionals in her firm. Fourteen months ago, she was overseeing a site inspection at a mid-rise residential project she had designed. Distracted by a phone call from a contractor and moving too quickly through an incompletely secured scaffold walkway, she failed to notice that a junior site engineer had followed her onto the platform. When she stepped back to gesture at a structural detail, she knocked him into a partially open stairwell. He fell nearly two storeys, fracturing his pelvis and shattering his left wrist. Adaeze heard the sound before she saw what had happened - a sharp crack of metal, then his voice cutting off mid-sentence into silence, then the dull concussion of impact below. She was the one who called the ambulance. She stood at the edge of the stairwell and watched the paramedics work, tasting the metallic coffee she had drunk that morning as though it had never left her mouth.

In the months that followed, the memory did not behave the way Adaeze expected memory to behave. When she tried deliberately to reconstruct the sequence of events - to understand exactly what she had done wrong - she found the account strangely inaccessible, fragmentary, resistant. Yet without warning, in the middle of a client presentation or lying beside her husband at night, the memory would return in pieces she had not chosen: the crack of the scaffold, the engineer's voice stopping, the taste of cold coffee flooding her mouth, and sometimes his cry from below rendered so precisely in her mind that she would turn her head, certain someone nearby had called out. These unbidden intrusions carried with them a quality of present-tense danger that her conscious knowledge of safety could not override, and she would find herself scanning the room, heart accelerating, certain that something was about to go wrong - even in her own kitchen, even at her desk. The intrusive sensory return of the memory was reliably triggering a state of alarm, and in that alarmed state she found the images intensified rather than resolved, the sounds sharpening rather than fading.

Adaeze had come to believe, with a conviction that felt irrefutable, that another architect - a more careful one, a better one - simply would not have been on that walkway distracted, would not have moved without checking. This belief sat at the centre of everything. She began dwelling on every decision she had made that morning, rehearsing the chain of her failures in exhaustive detail, and this rumination seemed to pull the fragmented memory back into circulation, feeding its frequency rather than containing it. At the same time, she had developed a set of private mental rituals at work: before entering any construction site, she would silently count through a sequence of safety checks in a fixed order, and if interrupted she would start again, convinced that completing the ritual correctly was the only thing standing between her professional actions and another catastrophe. She told herself, on harder days, that at least the engineer had survived, that it could have been worse - but the comparison offered only seconds of relief before the self-recrimination resumed. These strategies, which she understood intellectually to be irrational, paradoxically kept the threat feeling immediate and the memory close to the surface, so that her body remained in a state of readiness that exhausted her.

The hypervigilance had spread. Ordinary sounds on site - a dropped tool, a shout across scaffolding - would send a jolt through her that left her shaking. She had reduced her site visits to the minimum her role permitted, delegating walk-throughs to junior colleagues and offering professional reasons that were not entirely false but were not the whole truth. Her husband had noticed the withdrawal; she felt unable to explain to him, or to anyone, the person she had become, and that incapacity deepened her sense of isolation. The woman who had once moved through construction sites with quiet authority felt unrecognisable to her now.

What finally brought Adaeze to seek help was a meeting with the recovered engineer - a routine professional encounter, months after his return to work. She heard his voice in the corridor before she saw him, and her body responded as though the fall were happening again. She sat in her car for forty minutes afterward, unable to drive. She came to her first session hoping, above everything, to feel like herself again - and afraid that she no longer knew who that was.
